Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex EV Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then two. Today's conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Johnson:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex EV's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Mike Rivera, CEO; Sarah Chen, CFO; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike Rivera.

Mike Rivera:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 2024 was a pivotal quarter for Apex EV. We made significant strides in key areas, including ramping production volumes and capacity utilization, delivering record gross margins per vehicle, strengthening our order backlog and reservation trends, and sharpening our strategic outlook and priorities. We are particularly excited about the upcoming ramp of the Apex Cybertruck and its anticipated boost to our pickup segment market share, positioning us to challenge leaders like Tesla's Cybertruck and Rivian's R1T.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Chen to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Sarah Chen:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning, everyone. For Q3 2024, our revenue was $6.8 billion, representing a 152% increase year-over-year. Our gross margin was 22.4%, and our operating expenses were $1.1 billion. Net income was $520 million. We are maintaining a strong balance sheet with $4.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. Our guidance for next quarter is revenue of $8.2 billion to $8.7 billion, with automotive gross margins expanding toward 24%.

I'd like to dive deep into one of our key profitability metrics: gross margin per vehicle. For those joining us who may not be steeped in the auto sector, gross margin per vehicle is calculated as our average selling price, or ASP, per unit minus the cost of goods sold, or COGS, per unit. It's a critical leading indicator of our manufacturing efficiency, pricing power, and path to sustainable free cash flow generation in the hyper-competitive EV landscape.

Let me start with the headline numbers for Q3 2024. We delivered a record gross margin per vehicle of $14,200, up 27% year-over-year from $11,200 in Q3 2023, and up 8% quarter-over-quarter from $13,150 in Q2. This represents an all-time high for Apex EV, pushing our overall automotive gross margin to 22.4%—well above the industry average of around 12% for legacy OEMs like Ford and GM in their EV divisions, and closing the gap with Tesla's impressive 19.8% in their latest quarter.

Breaking this down, our ASP came in at $52,800 per vehicle, a 12% YoY increase driven by a richer product mix. Deliveries of our flagship Apex Pro sedan—our direct competitor to the Tesla Model S Plaid—surged 45% YoY to 18,000 units, pulling the average up with its $78,500 sticker price, bolstered by premium options like our next-gen 800V architecture and Level 3 autonomy hardware. Meanwhile, our more affordable Apex Compact, akin to a souped-up Bolt EUV, held steady at $42,000 ASP but gained traction in fleet sales to Uber and Hertz, comprising 35% of volume. Regulatory credits added another $1,200 per vehicle, similar to Tesla's ZEV credit windfall, though we're being conservative on future recognition amid evolving EPA rules.

On the COGS side, we shaved $3,900 per vehicle YoY, bringing it to $38,600. This is where our technical initiatives are really paying off. Battery costs, which still represent 35% of COGS, dropped 22% to $13,500 per pack thanks to the ramp of our in-house 4680 cylindrical cells at Gigafactory Nevada. These cells deliver 16% higher energy density than our prior 2170s, enabling a 20% range boost in the Apex Pro without added weight—critical for consumer pull in a market where EPA-rated range is king. We've also vertically integrated rare earth-free permanent magnet motors, cutting motor and inverter COGS by 18% to $4,200 per vehicle, leapfrogging suppliers like Bosch and Magna.

Factory utilization hit 92% across our U.S. and Berlin plants, generating $250 million in fixed cost absorption benefits—economies of scale that legacy players like Stellantis are still chasing with their tepid 65% EV plant loads. Our structural battery pack design, inspired by but improving on Tesla's, reduces SKU complexity by 40%, slashing assembly time to 9.5 hours per vehicle from 12 hours last year.

Regionally, the story varies. In North America, which accounted for 62% of deliveries, gross margin per vehicle hit $16,800—buoyed by IRA incentives averaging $4,500 per vehicle via our U.S.-sourced LFP batteries qualifying for the full $7,500 tax credit. Europe, at 25% of volume, came in at $13,200, pressured by softer pricing in Germany amid BYD's aggressive Seagull push, but offset by strong uptake of our Apex SUV in the UK with VAT rebates. China, our 13% exposure, lagged at $10,500 due to fierce price wars—think Xiaomi's SU7 undercutting us by 15%—but we're gaining share with localized Apex Compact production in Shanghai, targeting 25% margin expansion by Q1 2025 through tariff avoidance.

Strategically, these gains underscore our "Fortress Margin" playbook: relentless vertical integration to insulate against supply chain volatility, like the lithium price spike earlier this year, and software monetization. Full Apex Autonomy subscriptions, our FSD equivalent, now attach to 42% of vehicles at $199/month, contributing $800 in non-dilutive margin per subbed unit via over-the-air updates—no hardware COGS hit. We're on track for 25% company-wide gross margins by year-end 2025, outpacing Rivian's projected 15% and Lucid's ongoing sub-10% struggles, by launching the $35k Apex Lite in H1 with a sub-$25k COGS target through cell-to-pack tech.

Looking ahead, Q4 guidance embeds $14,800 gross margin per vehicle, assuming 15% volume growth to 120,000 units and stable ASP amid potential Fed rate cuts boosting affordability. Risks include battery metal hedging—we've locked in 80% of 2025 cathode needs—and China mix, but our U.S.-centric supply chain de-risks us versus Tesla's Shanghai reliance.

In summary, gross margin per vehicle isn't just a number—it's our moat in an industry where Ford's Model e lost $1.1 billion last quarter on razor-thin per-unit economics. We're executing flawlessly, and this sets us up for FCF positivity in Q4.

Building on that efficiency, let's turn to our production volume and capacity utilization rates, which were standout performers this quarter and underscore the scalability of our EV platform. In Q3, we produced 128,500 vehicles across our global footprint, marking a 142% year-over-year increase from the 53,000 units in Q3 2023. This puts our nine-month cumulative production at around 376,500 vehicles, on track for our full-year guidance of 550,000 to 600,000 units. Deliveries closely tracked production at 125,200 vehicles, with a 2.6% build-to-delivery mismatch primarily due to logistics in Europe amid Red Sea disruptions. For context, this volume growth outpaced the broader EV market, which saw global production up about 25% YoY per EV Volumes data, driven by our focus on high-margin CUVs and trucks amid softening sedan demand.

Breaking it down by model mix—a critical metric in our industry where ASPs vary wildly: The Apex X SUV, our volume leader comparable to the Tesla Model Y, saw 72,000 units produced, up 165% YoY, reflecting surging U.S. demand for family haulers bolstered by IRA-compliant battery sourcing. The Apex T Pickup, our F-150 Lightning rival, hit 38,500 units, a massive 220% YoY ramp from our new Texas Gigafactory line—we're now at full rate on the dual-motor AWD variant. The Apex S Sedan and Apex L Luxury combined for 18,000 units, flat YoY as we pivot capacity toward trucks amid Tesla's Cybertruck ramp and Ford's F-150 Lightning price cuts.

Capacity utilization rates hit 87% globally in Q3—up from 62% in Q3 2023 and 78% in Q2 2024. This is elite territory; for reference, Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory ran at about 92% in their latest quarter per their 10-Q, while legacy OEMs like GM hover around 70-75% on EV lines due to slower ramps. Our utilization reflects disciplined capex allocation and vertical integration, minimizing the "valley of death" many startups face post-SPAC.

Facility-by-facility: Nevada Gigafactory 1, with installed capacity of 300,000 vehicles and 40 GWh cells annually, produced 52,000 vehicles at 92% utilization, up 28 percentage points YoY. Texas Gigafactory, at 250,000 vehicles and 30 GWh, delivered 41,000 vehicles at 89%—a new site achievement. Georgia Gigafactory, 200,000 vehicles and 25 GWh, hit 22,500 vehicles at 76%, up 15 points. Europe Assembly in our Berlin JV, 100,000 vehicles capacity, produced 13,000 at 71%, up 10 points. Total: 850,000 vehicle capacity, 128,500 produced, 87% utilization, up 25 points YoY.

Nevada's near-92% on 2170 and prismatic LFP lines stems from WHMI improvements—we've boosted energy density to 280 Wh/kg via in-house cathode R&D, reducing scrap rates to under 1.5%. Texas hit 89% thanks to our proprietary structural battery pack, cutting weld points by 40% and enabling 10% faster takt times. Georgia's 76% is transitional; we're commissioning a second body-in-white line for Apex X RWD, targeting 85% by Q4. Europe's 71% reflects softer EU demand, down 12% YoY per ACEA, and homologation delays on 800V architecture, but we're mitigating with OTA updates mirroring Tesla's playbook.

Key trends and drivers: Production accelerated sequentially from Q2's 119,500 units, fueled by supply chain de-risking. Semiconductor yields hit 98% post-TSMC allocation, and cathode material costs dropped 22% YoY via Nevada upstream partnerships like Glencore-style offtakes for nickel-manganese. Inventory drawdown was minimal at 3,200 units, or 2.5% of production, far below Rivian's 10%+ overhang, preserving pricing power with Q3 ASP at $58,200.

Challenges? We navigated battery cell shortages early via qualifying LG's 46-series packs and ramping 4680 pilot to 5 GWh annualized. Utilization dipped to 82% in July before rebounding, compressing the EV ramp S-curve from 18 to 12 months via digital twins and AI-driven line balancing, akin to Tesla's factory automation.

Regionally: North America, 82% of volume, 105,000 units at 91% utilization—IRA Section 30D credits averaging $7,500 per vehicle drove 30% YoY retail growth, fleet sales to Hertz and Enterprise up 50%. Europe, 10%, 13,000 units pressured by 20% EV registration drop per JATO from subsidy phase-outs, countered by €200M Berlin expansion for right-hand-drive Apex X targeting UK/Ireland. Asia-Pacific, 8%, 10,500 units from Shanghai tolling—China up 80% YoY despite BYD price wars, 65% utilization export-focused to SEA's 40% EV CAGR.

Technical initiatives: "Factory 2.0" rollout with unboxed process like Tesla's Cybercab, reducing manufacturing cost 50% to $35k per vehicle; Giga Press Gen 3, 9,000-ton units casting rear underbody in one piece, boosting throughput 25%; 60% in-house content shielding from disruptions; 95% renewable energy, Nevada 100% solar for EU CBAM compliance.

Strategically, at 87% utilization, we're generating $1.2 billion in Q3 manufacturing cash flow, funding $2.5B capex for 1.2M annual capacity by 2026—including Mexico Giga for NAFTA optimization. This positions us for 5% U.S. EV share from 2.5% as Tesla Model 2 delays and GM Ultium bottlenecks create opportunity. Risks like UAW effects or China tariffs mitigated by 75% NA content. Margins at 18.5% gross on volume leverage.

Q4 production guidance: 145,000 to 155,000 units at 89-91% utilization.

Next, our order backlog and reservation trends continue to reflect robust underlying demand for our full-stack EV portfolio amid a dynamic macroeconomic and regulatory landscape. As of September 30th, our global order backlog stood at $18.7 billion, a 22% increase quarter-over-quarter from $15.3 billion at Q2 end, and 45% year-over-year growth. This equates to approximately 285,000 vehicles at our current ASP of $65,600—up from $62,200 last quarter, driven by mix shift to higher-margin Apex X SUV and ramping Apex Cybertruck. Weighted average delivery timeframe is now 14 weeks, down from 18 in Q2, signaling improved throughput at Fremont and Spartanburg Gigafactories.

Reservation trends: 420,000 fully refundable reservations end-Q3, up 15% sequentially and 38% YoY. Conversion to firm orders hit 68%—our highest—bolstered by app-based configurator and Ally Financial integrations. Apex Cybertruck holds 180,000 reservations, 45,000 converting in Q3, outperforming Tesla's early 30% amid our supply resolve.

By model: Apex S sedan backlog 65,000 units flat QoQ, reservations up 12% to 95,000 on OTA Level 3 autonomy via ApexMind neural net—98.5% disengagement-free in CA DMV. Apex X SUV backlog up 35% to 140,000, reservations 25% to 210,000 on 520-mile Long Range Plus with 4680 cells, COGS down 18%. Apex Cybertruck backlog doubled to 80,000, reservations 180,000, efficiency 2.8 miles/kWh beating Rivian.

Regionally: North America, 72% backlog up 28% to $13.5B on IRA—$7,500 rebates, $45/kWh credits accelerated Uber/Hertz fleets by 25,000 units; reservations up 20% despite credit front-loading. Europe, 18%, up 8% to $3.4B, reservations down 5% to 55,000 on subsidy cuts—countered by Berlin LFP swaps for sub-€40k Apex S like BYD. Asia-Pacific, 10%, up 40% to $1.8B, China reservations doubled to 70,000 on Shanghai JV dual-motor AWD vs NIO/XPeng.

Drivers: EV adoption at 22% U.S. share per Cox; 800V 10-min charges, ApexOS 4.2 FSD beta waitlists 100k+. Supply: 4680 yields 92% from 75%, enabling 52,000 Q3 deliveries, 40% QoQ ramp. Optimizing by pruning low-conversion 10% via AI, dynamic pricing 5% premium on Cybertruck Foundation Series amid steel inflation—for $2.5B FCF from fulfillment at 85% margins.

Forward: $20+ billion backlog year-end, Q4 reservations to 500k on Cybertruck Tri-Motor "Beast" and India Tata partnership. Risks: LFP tariffs, sentiment—but 60% U.S. content, software moat resilient vs Ford Lightning cuts.

With that comprehensive view of our financials, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs.

Analyst 1:
Thanks, and congrats on the strong quarter. On gross margins per vehicle, can you elaborate on the sustainability given commodity volatility and potential pricing pressure in China?

Mike Rivera:
Thanks, John. Absolutely, our $14,200 gross margin per vehicle is built on a fortress-like structure. We've locked 80% of 2025 cathode needs and our vertical integration—60% in-house including 4680 cells and rare earth-free motors—insulates us from lithium spikes. In China, localized Shanghai production avoids tariffs and targets 25% expansion by Q1 2025. Software like Apex Autonomy at 42% attach adds $800 non-dilutive margin. We're guiding $14,800 for Q4 with 15% volume uptick, confident in 25% company-wide by 2025 end.

Operator:
Our next question from Lisa Chen with Morgan Stanley.

Analyst 2:
Great results. On production, with 87% global utilization, what are the key risks to hitting Q4 guidance of 145k-155k units, especially in Europe and new sites like Texas?

Sarah Chen:
Thanks, Lisa. Risks are manageable. Texas is already at 89% post-six-month ramp, thanks to structural packs and Giga Press boosting throughput 25%. Europe at 71% faces demand softness from subsidy phase-outs, but Berlin expansion for RHD Apex X mitigates. We've de-risked supply with 98% semi yields and LG 46-series quals. The S-curve is compressed to 12 months via AI balancing—no major macro shocks assumed, positioning for 1.2M capacity by 2026.

Operator:
Next from David Kim with Barclays.

Analyst 3:
Impressive backlog growth to $18.7B. How do you view reservation conversion trends into 2025, particularly for Cybertruck amid competition?

Mike Rivera:
David, thanks. 68% Q3 conversion is record, driven by resolved 4680 yields to 92% and OTA features like ApexMind Level 3. Cybertruck's 180k reservations converting at higher rates than Tesla's early figures, with 2.8 miles/kWh efficiency edge. We're pruning low-conversion via AI, guiding to 500k Q4 reservations and $20B+ backlog year-end, resilient with dynamic pricing and India entry.

Alex Johnson:
Thank you for your questions. We have time for one more.

Operator:
Our final question from Rachel Patel with JPMorgan.

Analyst 4:
On capex and priorities, how does the $2.5B plan align with FCF positivity and regional expansion?

Sarah Chen:
Rachel, spot on. The $2.5B funds Mexico Giga for USMCA and Southeast Asia LFP with CATL for $45/kWh cells. It supports 500k-600k FY deliveries, generating $1.2B quarterly manufacturing cash flow already. FCF positive Q4, H2 2025 at $300M+ for buybacks if EPS beats. 75% NA content hedges tariffs, renewables hit 95% for CBAM.

Operator:
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Mike Rivera for closing remarks.

Mike Rivera:
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. As we wrap up a transformative Q3 with record 125,000 deliveries—up 65% YoY—and gross margins at 22.4% on optimized LFP-NMC packs, let's focus on the strategic outlook for Q4 2024 and fiscal 2025. Priorities center on scaling sustainably, profitability, and share capture amid softening demand and trade tensions.

Four pillars: First, production ramp and capacity. Reno Nevada at 85% utilization, 35k/month on Apex Pro and Compact. $1.8B 2025 capex, $1.2B for Spartanburg Gigafactory breaking ground January—50 GWh 4680 cells, 15% denser, 20% cheaper kWh. CATL LFP localization in SEA cuts costs 25%. Q4 40k units, Q1 2025 45k clearing inventory.

Second, product innovation. V10 pickup Q2 2025 vs Cybertruck/R1T: 500-mile range, 800V, 11kW V2G offsetting 30% grid costs, $68k pre-IRA, 25k pre-orders. V4 hatch Q1 Level 3 with NVIDIA Orin-X 1,000 TOPS half Waymo cost. V6 400V LFP for fleets, 25% ICE TCO edge. R&D 8% revenue ($450M), 40% solid-state—400 Wh/kg prototypes with QuantumScape for 2027 600-mile, 10-min charges.

Third, regional penetration. North America 60% volumes on IRA—65% U.S. content, 5k Supercharger stalls 350kW, 20% pickup share. Europe 25%, RHD V8 UK Q1, 40% growth on CO2-compliant V6. China 10-15%, RMB150k V4 Shanghai JV with Huawei autonomy vs BYD Seagull/Xiaomi. India/Brazil 5% CKD.

Fourth, resilience and discipline. Q4 margins 23.5%, 28% 2025 end via 70% power electronics insource, 95% UPH. FCF positive H2 2025 $300M, $500M buybacks. Hedged 80% lithium $12k/tonne, $4.2B cash, $1.5B revolver.

2025: 500k deliveries, 28% margins, positive FCF, long-range EV leadership. We're engineering mobility's future. We are confident that Apex EV is well-positioned for continued success in the rapidly evolving automotive landscape. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter.

Alex Johnson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the Apex EV Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
